title_en: Kaidefu International Trade (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. v. Kuosheng Pipeline System (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over trademark infringement and false advertising
ruling_gist_en: An operator's use of another's registered trademark to explain the change of brand authorized distributors, within the scope of good faith and reasonable limits, constitutes fair use of the trademark and does not constitute trademark infringement. Where the new distributor truthfully and in detail informs consumers of the change of product distributor and brand, the new distributor's use of the former distributor's registered trademark in promotion will not cause misunderstanding among the relevant public and does not constitute false advertising.

full_text_en:
Kaidefu International Trade (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. v. Kuo Sheng Piping Systems (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over trademark infringement and false publicity

[Ruling Summary]

Where an operator uses another's registered trademark within the bounds of good faith and reasonableness for the purpose of explaining a change in the brand's authorized distributor, such use constitutes fair use of the trademark and does not constitute trademark infringement. Where a new distributor truthfully and in detail informs consumers of the change in the sales agent and brand, the new distributor's use of the former distributor's registered trademark in its publicity will not cause the relevant public to misunderstand and does not constitute false publicity.

Plaintiff: Kaidefu International Trade (Shanghai) Co., Ltd., domiciled at Aona Road, China (Shanghai) Pilot Free Trade Zone.
Legal Representative: Volker Scheel, General Manager of the company.

Defendant: Kuo Sheng Piping Systems (Shanghai) Co., Ltd., domiciled at Guanshengyuan Road, Xuhui District, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Zhou Wenhao, Executive Director of the company.

Defendant: Shanghai Ousu Trading Co., Ltd., domiciled at Gubei North Road, Songjiang District, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Ji Shunyuan, General Manager of the company.

Plaintiff Kaidefu International Trade (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Kaidefu) filed a lawsuit with the Xuhui District People's Court of Shanghai against Defendants Kuo Sheng Piping Systems (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Kuo Sheng) and Shanghai Ousu Trading Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Ousu) concerning a dispute over trademark infringement and false publicity.

Plaintiff's Allegations: The promotional phrases used by Defendants Kuo Sheng and Ousu, such as "Originally German Jieshui, now German Kuo Sheng" and "German Kuo Sheng (formerly German Jieshui) — Unchanging Quality," among similar expressions, contain the "Jieshui" trademark, constituting trademark infringement against the Plaintiff. Furthermore, these promotional phrases are capable of misleading consumers and constitute false publicity. Therefore, the Plaintiff filed the lawsuit, requesting the court to order: 1. Kuo Sheng to cease using advertising language identical or similar in meaning to "Originally German Jieshui" and "German Jieshui has changed its name to German Kuo Sheng" in its external publicity, promotion, and sales activities, which constitute unfair competition through false publicity; to destroy, withdraw, and eliminate promotional materials, billboards, and other promotional items containing such advertising language; and to cease publishing such advertisements on relevant websites, web pages, newspapers, notices, etc.; Ousu to cease using advertising language identical or similar in meaning to "Originally German Jieshui," "Old German Jieshui," and "German Jieshui has changed its name to German Kuo Sheng" in its external publicity, promotion, and sales activities, which constitute unfair competition through false publicity; to destroy, withdraw, and eliminate construction contact sheets, promotional materials, billboards, and other promotional items containing such advertising language; 2. Kuo Sheng and Ousu to cease infringing the exclusive right to use the registered trademark "Jieshui" (Registration No. 1720019) owned by Kaidefu; 3. Kuo Sheng to publish an apology to Kaidefu in prominent positions in *Yangtze Evening Post* and *Xinmin Evening News*, as well as on the homepages of the websites NanTaiHu.net, Sina.com, 58.com, Hexun.com, and the Shanghai Building Materials Industry Association website, with the content subject to court review and the costs borne by Kuo Sheng; 4. Kuo Sheng to make positive publicity for the registered trademark "Jieshui" in prominent positions in *Yangtze Evening Post* and *Xinmin Evening News*, as well as on the homepages of the websites NanTaiHu.net, Sina.com, 58.com, Hexun.com, and the Shanghai Building Materials Industry Association website, to eliminate the adverse effects caused by its trademark infringement and unfair competition acts on Kaidefu, with the content subject to court review and the costs borne by Kuo Sheng; 5. Kuo Sheng and Ousu to jointly and severally compensate Kaidefu for economic losses and reasonable expenses totaling RMB 5,000,000 (including legal representation fees of RMB 413,000 and notarization fees of RMB 14,000); 6. Court acceptance fees and preservation application fees to be jointly borne by Kuo Sheng and Ousu.

Defendant Kuo Sheng's Defense: 1. The reputation of Plaintiff Kaidefu's "Jieshui" trademark was built upon the products of Aquatherm GmbH that Kaidefu distributed. Since July 1, 2013, Kaidefu lost its distribution rights. The "Jieshui" trademark is no longer associated with Aquatherm GmbH's products, and Kaidefu may no longer use "German Jieshui" for promotion; 2. The objective reports by websites and media to prevent confusion among relevant consumers were not acts of Kuo Sheng; 3. False publicity pertains to the goods themselves. Even if the court finds that Kuo Sheng used the advertising phrases alleged by Kaidefu, it does not constitute false publicity; 4. Kuo Sheng and Ousu had neither joint intent to infringe nor jointly committed any infringing acts. Kuo Sheng requests the court to dismiss all of Kaidefu's claims.

Defendant Ousu's Defense: Since July 1, 2013, after Plaintiff Kaidefu lost its distribution rights, the manufacturer and place of origin of the products sold changed, but Defendant Kaidefu failed to inform the relevant market and consumers. As Kuo Sheng's regional general agent for Shanghai, Ousu continued to sell Aquatherm GmbH's products. The internal promotional materials distributed to downstream dealers in the course of business merely objectively indicated that the distribution entity for Aquatherm GmbH's products had changed. Subjectively, there was no fault, and objectively, no consumer confusion was caused. There was no act of false publicity. Ousu requests the court to dismiss all of Kaidefu's claims.

Facts Found by the Xuhui District People's Court of Shanghai at First Instance:

Plaintiff Kaidefu is the owner of the word mark "Jieshui," which was approved for registration in 2002, covering goods in Class 17, including plastic pipes. On April 6, 2006, Kaidefu entered into an exclusive distribution agreement with the German company Aquatherm GmbH, granting Kaidefu exclusive distribution rights in China for Aquatherm GmbH's pipe products. The German company Aquatherm GmbH had registered in China the trademarks "" and "aquatherm" for goods in Class 19, including drainage installations. On June 30, 2013, Kaidefu and Aquatherm GmbH terminated their cooperation agreement, and Kaidefu ceased to act as the distributor of Aquatherm GmbH's products. On July 1, 2013, Defendant Kuo Sheng became the new distributor in China for Aquatherm GmbH's products. Prior to July 1, 2013, Kaidefu's registered trademark "Jieshui" was used exclusively to promote and sell Aquatherm GmbH's products. After July 1, 2013, Kaidefu continued to hold the "Jieshui" trademark, which it used to promote pipe products of other manufacturers. After obtaining the distribution rights for Aquatherm GmbH's products, Kuo Sheng authorized Defendant Ousu to be the exclusive distributor of Aquatherm GmbH's products in the Shanghai region. In articles on third-party websites and in promotional materials of Kuo Sheng and Ousu, phrases such as "Originally German Jieshui, now German Kuo Sheng," "German Kuo Sheng (formerly German Jieshui) — Unchanging Quality," and "aquatherm (formerly German Jieshui) German Kuo Sheng" appeared. When using these promotional phrases, they also included statements such as "The former distributor once promoted the products in China under the name 'German Jieshui.' Starting July 1, the German manufacturer officially adopted the Chinese designation 'Kuo Sheng' for promotion in the Chinese market," and "German aquatherm GmbH officially adopted its officially held Chinese designation 'Kuo Sheng' for market promotion in China starting July 1, 2013. The previously used Chinese designation 'Jieshui' in China was held by the former distributor and now has no connection whatsoever with German Kuo Sheng aquatherm GmbH and its products." Kuo Sheng set up links on its operated website to the promotional content of these third-party websites.

Opinion of the Xuhui District People's Court of Shanghai at First Instance:

The issues in dispute at first instance were: 1. Whether the alleged infringing acts complained of by Plaintiff Kaidefu were all related to Defendants Kuo Sheng and Ousu; 2. Whether Kuo Sheng and Ousu infringed the exclusive right to use the registered trademark "Jieshui" owned by Kaidefu; 3. Whether Kaidefu's claim that Kuo Sheng and Ousu engaged in false publicity was established.

Regarding Issue 1. Defendant Kuo Sheng argued that although it had set up links on its operated website to articles stored on other websites, those articles were published by others and it should not bear liability. The first-instance court held that even if Kuo Sheng did not publish those articles, by setting up links on its operated website, it directed users visiting its website to read them, objectively used those articles for promotion, and indicated to the relevant public that it agreed with the viewpoints in the articles. Therefore, the first-instance court found that the above articles were related to Kuo Sheng.

Defendant Ousu argued that the relevant promotional materials were internal materials not intended for consumers and should not give rise to liability. The court found that, based on facts recorded in the relevant notarized documents, the above materials were not marked with "Internal Materials" or "Do Not Disclose." Moreover, when Plaintiff Kaidefu's agent ad litem purchased the relevant products, they were able to obtain the above materials as an ordinary consumer. Therefore, Ousu's statement contradicted the objective facts, and the court did not accept it.

As for the remaining alleged infringing acts complained of by Plaintiff Kaidefu, given that Defendants Kuo Sheng and Ousu denied having committed them, Kaidefu bore the burden of proof. Kaidefu failed to provide sufficient evidence during the first-instance proceedings. The first-instance court did not support these claims.

Regarding Issue 2. The court found that the articles and promotional materials in question indeed contained the word "Jieshui." However, analyzing the specific circumstances in which the word "Jieshui" was used — for example, "The previously used Chinese designation 'Jieshui' in China was held by the former distributor" and "The former distributor once promoted the products in China under the name 'German Jieshui'" — it is clear to the relevant public that the "Jieshui" trademark refers to Kaidefu. There is no likelihood of confusion or mistake. The use of "Jieshui" in these instances should be considered fair use. Therefore, the first-instance court did not support Kaidefu's claim that Kuo Sheng and Ousu infringed its exclusive right to use the registered trademark "Jieshui."

Regarding Issue 3. The court found that although the content of the articles and promotional materials contained phrases such as "Originally German Jieshui," "Old German Jieshui," and "Originally German 'Jieshui,' now German 'Kuo Sheng,'" the determination of whether this constitutes false publicity should be made by considering factors such as common experience in daily life, the general attention of the relevant public, the fact of misunderstanding, and the actual situation of the advertised subject matter when assessing misleading false publicity.

First, prior to July 1, 2013, Plaintiff Kaidefu used the "Jieshui" trademark solely to promote and sell Aquatherm GmbH's products. The "Jieshui" trademark had established an extremely close connection with Aquatherm GmbH's products and trademarks. For the relevant public, the "Jieshui" trademark referred to Aquatherm GmbH's products. Therefore, the phrases "Originally German Jieshui" and "Old German Jieshui" were factually accurate and not false statements.

Second, the words in the articles and promotional materials in question must not be interpreted in isolation but as a whole. The relevant promotional content explained the background of the change in the agency relationship. After applying ordinary attention to reading this content, the relevant public would not be misled by the phrases "Originally German Jieshui," "Old German Jieshui," and "Originally German 'Jieshui,' now German 'Kuo Sheng,'" nor would they misunderstand the relationship between the two.

Finally, given that Plaintiff Kaidefu, when serving as the general agent in China for Aquatherm GmbH, had established an extremely close connection between the "Jieshui" trademark and Aquatherm GmbH's products, when important matters such as the change of distributors and the discontinuation of the former distributor's trademark for promotional purposes occurred, Aquatherm GmbH, Kaidefu, and Kuo Sheng should have accurately and promptly disclosed these important matters to ensure the right to know of the relevant public.

Since Plaintiff Kaidefu failed to prove that Defendants Kuo Sheng and Ousu had infringed its exclusive right to use the registered trademark "Jieshui" or constituted false publicity, the first-instance court also did not support Kaidefu's claims for cessation of infringement, apology, elimination of adverse effects, and compensation for economic losses.

Accordingly, pursuant to Article 48 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 9(1) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 8 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in Adjudicating Civil Cases Involving Unfair Competition, Article 9 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Issues Concerning the Jurisdiction and Application of Law in Trademark Cases After the Implementation of the Decision on Amending the Trademark Law, and Article 90 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, on March 13, 2015, the Xuhui District People's Court of Shanghai rendered the following judgment:

All claims of Plaintiff Kaidefu were dismissed.

Kaidefu, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Shanghai Intellectual Property Court, arguing: 1. The two appellees' use of the "Jieshui" trademark was not fair use; their use would cause consumers to be confused as to the source of the goods, constituting trademark infringement. 2. The appellees' purpose in using "Jieshui" was to ride on the goodwill of the appellant's trademark, not to ensure consumers' right to know. 3. The appellees' use of "Jieshui" in their publicity had already caused consumer misunderstanding, constituting false publicity.

Appellee Kuo Sheng argued: 1. After Appellant Kaidefu terminated its agency relationship with Aquatherm GmbH, Kuo Sheng, as the new distributor, had an obligation to inform consumers of this situation. The relevant advertising and promotional language was not intended to ride on the appellant's registered trademark but to prevent consumers from being misled as to the source of the goods.

Appellee Ousu agreed with Kuo Sheng's defense and added: 1. Before July 1, 2013, Appellant Kaidefu used the "Jieshui" trademark solely to promote and market Aquatherm GmbH's pipe products. Therefore, consumers recognized Aquatherm GmbH's pipe products, not the "Jieshui" trademark itself. 3. Given the change in distribution rights, Ousu, as a distributor, merely informed consumers of this change, which constitutes fair use of the trademark.

Upon second instance, the Shanghai Intellectual Property Court confirmed the facts found at first instance.

Opinion of the Shanghai Intellectual Property Court at Second Instance:

The issues in dispute in the second instance were primarily two: 1. Whether the conduct of Appellees Kuo Sheng and Ousu constituted trademark infringement; 2. Whether the conduct of Kuo Sheng and Ousu constituted false publicity.

I. Whether the conduct of Appellees Kuo Sheng and Ousu constituted trademark infringement

The basic function of a trademark is to distinguish the source of goods or services. In determining whether a business operator's use of another's trademark in commercial activities constitutes trademark infringement, consideration should be given to whether the specific use destroys the function of the trademark to connect with the goods or services — that is, whether it would cause the relevant public to be confused as to the source of the goods or services. If the use of another's trademark in commercial activities is merely to describe or explain some objective situation and does not cause the relevant public to be confused as to the source of the goods or services, then such use is not trademark use within the meaning of the Trademark Law but rather fair use of the trademark, which the trademark owner has no right to prohibit. In this case, the two appellees' use in their promotional activities of phrases such as "German Kuo Sheng (formerly German Jieshui) — Unchanging Quality" and "Originally German Jieshui, now German Kuo Sheng" does not constitute trademark infringement, primarily for the following reasons:

First, the two appellees' use of the "Jieshui" trademark was subjective in good faith. Before July 1, 2013, the appellant used the "Jieshui" trademark solely to promote and sell Aquatherm GmbH's products. The trademark had established a stable and exclusive connection with Aquatherm GmbH's products. In the cognition of relevant consumers, the "Jieshui" trademark referred to Aquatherm GmbH's products. After July 1, 2013, the distributor of Aquatherm GmbH's products in China changed from Appellant Kaidefu to Appellee Kuo Sheng. Based on the fact that the "Jieshui" trademark had established a stable connection with Aquatherm GmbH's products, the two appellees had a necessary need in their promotional activities to inform consumers that the product previously referred to by the "Jieshui" trademark had changed. Therefore, the appellees' use of the "Jieshui" trademark in their promotional language was subjectively not intended to ride on the appellant's goodwill but was necessary to describe objective facts.

Second, the manner in which the two appellees used the "Jieshui" trademark was reasonable and would not cause confusion among relevant consumers. The appellees had already provided detailed information to consumers about the background of the change in product distributor and brand. When consumers read the appellees' promotional language, they would typically understand that the products sold by Kuo Sheng were the products previously referred to by the "Jieshui" trademark, i.e., Aquatherm GmbH's products, and would not be confused as to the source of the goods.

In summary, the two appellees' use of the "Jieshui" trademark in their promotional activities constitutes fair use and does not constitute trademark infringement.

II. Whether the conduct of Appellees Kuo Sheng and Ousu constituted false publicity

The false publicity regulated by the Anti-Unfair Competition Law refers to "misleading" false publicity. Only when the promotional content has the effect of misleading does it harm fair competition in the market and the legitimate rights and interests of consumers. The determination of "misleading" false publicity should be made by comprehensively considering factors such as common experience in daily life, the general attention of the relevant public, the fact of misunderstanding, and the actual situation of the advertised subject matter.

In this case, first, the promotional language used by the two appellees should be interpreted as a whole. Consumers generally accept commercial promotion as a whole. In determining whether the promotional content has a misleading effect, the focus should be on whether the content as a whole is likely to cause misunderstanding to the relevant public; individual words or sentences that might be taken out of context should not be isolated. Even if part of the promotional content, when analyzed in isolation, could be ambiguous, if consumers, after receiving the whole, can dispel the ambiguity, then there is essentially no misleading effect. As previously noted, when using the allegedly infringing promotional language, the two appellees also detailed the background of the change in product distributor and brand. Therefore, the phrases that appellant Kaidefu claimed constituted false publicity cannot be judged in isolation from the specific context but should be reasonably interpreted within the overall promotional content.

Second, the determination should be made based on the general attention of the relevant public, their existing knowledge and experience, and the actual situation of the advertised subject matter. Whether promotional content will mislead the audience's transactional decisions is closely related to the audience's own existing knowledge and experience. Since the two appellees, when using the allegedly infringing promotional language, had already detailed the background of the change in product distributor and brand, and given that consumers already have some cognitive experience with this brand's products, the relevant public, applying ordinary attention, should be able to understand the true meaning of the promotional content and would not be misled as to whether the "Jieshui" trademark itself had changed or the source of the goods sold by Kuo Sheng.

In summary, the publicity content of the two appellees did not produce any misleading effect and does not constitute false publicity.

In conclusion, the acts of the two appellees do not constitute trademark infringement or false publicity. The first-instance judgment found clear facts, correctly applied the law, and rendered an appropriate decision. Accordingly, the Shanghai Intellectual Property Court, pursuant to Article 170, paragraph 1(1) and Article 175 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, on July 28, 2015, rendered the following judgment:

The appeal is dismissed and the original judgment is affirmed.

This judgment is final.
